runs.u: Which laptop brand would you pick?
runs.reply:
If I had to pick one, I'd probably go with **Apple** — the MacBook Air is arguably the best default laptop for most people: excellent battery life, strong performance, great build quality, and it holds its value well. But "best brand" really depends on what you're doing:

- **Business/work (Windows):** Lenovo ThinkPads — legendary keyboards, durable, and easy to repair
- **Gaming:** ASUS ROG/Zephyrus or Lenovo Legion — great performance for the price
- **Budget:** Acer or lower-tier Lenovo — fine for basics, just watch for bloatware and mediocre displays
- **Repairability/upgradability:** Framework — niche, but the only laptop you can genuinely fix and upgrade yourself

Dell and HP make solid machines too, but quality varies a lot across their lineups, so it's more model-dependent than brand-dependent.

One caveat: my knowledge goes up to early 2025, so newer releases may have shaken things up.

What do you mainly use a laptop for? I can narrow it down to a specific pick if you share your budget and use case.

runs.u: Which cloud provider would you pick?
runs.reply:
If I had to pick a single default with no other context: **AWS**. Not because it's the most pleasant to use, but because it's the safest bet—deepest service catalog, most mature ecosystem, best documentation and community knowledge, and the largest hiring pool if your team grows.

That said, the right answer depends a lot on your situation:

- **Microsoft shop** (Windows, .NET, Active Directory, Office 365)? → **Azure** integrates far better with that stack
- **Data/ML-heavy workloads**? → **GCP** — BigQuery, Vertex AI, and the best managed Kubernetes (GKE)
- **Small project, cost-sensitive**? → **DigitalOcean, Hetzner, or Vultr** — the big three get expensive fast at small scale, and their complexity is overkill
- **Just want to deploy an app, not manage servers**? → **Fly.io, Railway, or Render**

The factor that matters most in practice is your team's existing familiarity. Operator experience beats marginal feature differences almost every time—a team that knows Azure well will ship faster on Azure than on a "better" platform they don't know.

What are you building? I can give you a more specific recommendation if you share the workload, scale, and budget.

runs.u: Which payment app would you pick?
runs.reply:
If I had to pick just one for everyday use in the US, I'd go with **Venmo** — not because it's technically the best, but because network effects matter most: it's the app your friends, roommates, and the food truck are most likely to already have. An app nobody else uses is worthless no matter how good it is.

That said, the "right" pick really depends on the job:

- **Splitting bills with friends:** Venmo or Zelle (Zelle is free, instant, and goes straight between bank accounts)
- **Online shopping:** PayPal, for its buyer protection
- **In-store checkout:** Apple Pay or Google Pay — contactless is just faster and more secure
- **International transfers:** Wise, for near-market exchange rates and low fees

A few caveats worth knowing: Zelle has no fraud protection since it's basically instant cash, and Venmo's social feed defaults to showing your transactions publicly (you can and probably should switch that to private).

And if you're outside the US, this whole list goes out the window — it'd be Revolut, Pix, UPI, or whatever dominates your region instead.

What are you mainly looking to use it for? Happy to narrow it down.

runs.reply:
If I had to pick just one, I'd go with **Brooks**. They're a running-focused company, their shoes are consistent year to year (the Ghost is a beloved workhorse), and they tend to prioritize durability and fit over chasing trends.

That said, the "right" brand really depends on what you're after:

- **Racing/performance:** Nike (Vaporfly, Alphafly) or Adidas Adizero
- **Max cushion comfort:** Hoka (Clifton, Bondi)
- **Best value all-rounder:** Saucony Endorphin Speed
- **Roomy toe box / natural feel:** Altra or Topo

The honest truth though: fit beats brand every time. A mid-tier shoe that matches your foot shape and gait will serve you better than a top-rated shoe that doesn't.

What kind of running are you doing — daily training, racing, trails? I can narrow it down from there.

- **Linear** is fast and opinionated, with defaults good enough that you just use it instead of configuring it. Most PM tools drown you in setup; Linear mostly gets out of the way. The catch: it's really built for product development, not general use.
- **Asana** is the best general-purpose option — flexible enough for marketing, ops, or mixed teams, with solid list/board/timeline views and a polished UI.

A few situational alternatives:

- **Trello** — dead simple, great for small teams or personal projects
- **Notion** — if you want docs and projects living in one place and don't mind some setup
- **Jira** — fine for large orgs with established process; I'd avoid it otherwise, since the complexity rarely pays off for smaller teams

What kind of team and work is it for? Happy to narrow it down.

I don't have a phone myself, but if I were choosing today in the US, I'd probably go with **T-Mobile or a budget MVNO**. Here's my thinking:

- **T-Mobile** offers the best mix of fast urban 5G, competitive pricing, and decent perks like international roaming.
- **Verizon** still wins for rural coverage, so it's the safer bet if you're outside metro areas.
- **AT&T** sits solidly in the middle.
- The sleeper pick is an **MVNO** like Visible, Mint Mobile, or US Mobile — they run on the big three's networks at half the price or less. The main tradeoff is deprioritized data during congestion, which most people rarely notice.

The single biggest factor, though, is coverage where you actually live, work, and travel. A carrier that's great in one city can be terrible in another, so it's worth checking coverage maps or asking people nearby.

That said, I assumed US — if you're in the UK, Canada, or elsewhere, the answer changes completely. Where are you based, and how much data do you typically use?

runs.u: Which mobile carrier would you pick?
runs.reply:
If I were picking for myself, I'd probably go with an MVNO like Visible or Mint Mobile—they run on the big carriers' towers (Verizon's and T-Mobile's networks, respectively) but cost $25–35/month instead of $70+.

The main tradeoff is deprioritization: during network congestion, your speeds can slow down before postpaid customers'. For most people that's rare enough that the savings are well worth it.

The one case where I'd pay full price for a major carrier is if I lived somewhere rural or traveled through remote areas a lot—Verizon's rural coverage is genuinely better in much of the US, and having no signal makes any price irrelevant.

The real answer, though, is that coverage varies a lot by location, so the "best" carrier is whichever one has strong signal where you actually live, work, and commute. If you tell me where you are and what you care about most (price, data, coverage, perks), I can give you a more specific recommendation.

runs.u: Which mobile carrier would you pick?
runs.reply:
If I were picking for myself in the US, I'd probably go with T-Mobile for most situations—good coverage in cities and suburbs, fast mid-band 5G, and reasonable pricing with perks. But the honest answer depends on two things:

**Where you live matters most.** Verizon wins in rural areas; T-Mobile and AT&T can be spotty outside towns. Nothing beats checking a coverage map (or asking neighbors) for your specific location.

**Price sensitivity matters too.** If saving money is a priority, I'd skip the big carriers entirely and use an MVNO like Visible, Mint, or US Mobile. They run on the same networks—Verizon, T-Mobile, AT&T towers—but charge half the price. You give up some perks and customer service polish, but $25–30/month for solid unlimited service is hard to argue with.

So my pick: T-Mobile if I want the mainstream experience, US Mobile or Visible if I'm being budget-savvy, Verizon if I live somewhere remote.

Are you in the US, or somewhere else? And what's driving the decision—price, coverage, or plan perks?
